doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Big bands, jazz educators and television
summary: Young players lack big bands; educators keep jazz going and TV has hurt it.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah. It was different from Herschel you know? See that’s another thing about young players today. I was very fortunate man because I came up at the right time. I came up at the right time, and these young dudes today don’t — it’s totally impossible because you don’t have the bands. There’s nothing like a big band — experience in playing with a big band or listening to a big band, or breathing with a big band. There’s nothing like that experience. And thank goodness man, one thing I would say about the jazz educators throughout the universities, the schools, fortunately man, they’re doing everything they can to keep it going. Because outside of that, nothing. And unfortunately because the media won’t accept, you know, T.V. has done more to hurt the big bands, the big, broad sound, than it has to help them. T.V. has hurt jazz. Can you imagine if T.V. had devoted one-third of the time that they devote to this other kind of music? This what they refer to music. You know, people would still be into this form of music — I would say “form” of music.
In esssence, a family that listens to jazz together stays together.
